propositions.text: The Applicant seeks judicial review of a visa officer's refusal of her temporary work permit application under the Temporary Foreign Worker Program.
propositions.quote: The Applicant seeks judicial review of a visa officer’s decision to deny her application for a temporary work permit/visa under the Temporary Foreign Worker Program [the Program] in Canada.

propositions.text: The Applicant submits the visa officer's decision was unreasonable given credible evidence to the contrary.
propositions.quote: The Applicant submits that the visa officer’s decision was unreasonable in light of credible evidence to the contrary.

propositions.text: The Respondent disagrees with the Applicant's submission that the decision was unreasonable.
propositions.quote: The Respondent disagrees.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant seeks judicial review of a visa refusal, arguing unreasonableness; the Respondent disagrees, says the decision was reasonable.

propositions.text: The parties disagree whether the visa officer should have communicated with the Applicant to address concerns about her visa application.
propositions.quote: The parties also disagree as to whether the visa officer should have communicated with the Applicant to address concerns related to her visa application.

paragraphs.summary: The parties dispute whether the visa officer should have communicated with the Applicant about concerns.

propositions.text: The application for judicial review is allowed for reasons set out below.
propositions.quote: The application for judicial review is allowed for the reasons set out below.

paragraphs.summary: The court allows the judicial review application for reasons explained below.

propositions.text: The Applicant was born in 1991, is Nigerian, and worked as a childcare attendant in Nigeria from 2015 to 2018.
propositions.quote: The Applicant was born on October 22, 1991 and is a citizen of Nigeria. From March 2015 to December 2018, the Applicant worked as a childcare attendant at a group of schools in the Delta State/Effurun Sapele region of Nigeria.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant is a Nigerian born in 1991 who worked as a childcare attendant in Nigeria from 2015 to 2018.

propositions.text: In May 2018, the Applicant and prospective employer entered a contract for live-in caregiver work in Fort McMurray for 24 months, 44 hours per week.
propositions.quote: On May 14, 2018, the Applicant and her prospective employer, a resident of Fort McMurray, Alberta, entered into a Temporary Foreign Worker Program In-Home Caregiver Employer/Employee Contract [the Contract]. According to the terms of the Contract, the Applicant was to work as a live-in caregiver for the prospective employer’s two young children for a 24-month period at their home in Fort McMurray. The Applicant’s tasks would include childcare, light housekeeping and meal preparation. The Contract also specified that the Applicant would work 44 hours per week.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant contracted in May 2018 to work as a live-in caregiver in Fort McMurray for 24 months, 44 hours weekly.

propositions.text: The prospective employer applied for and received a positive Labour Market Impact Assessment for the Applicant's position in June 2018.
propositions.quote: On May 16, 2018, the prospective employer submitted a Labour Market Impact Assessment [LMIA] application for the position to be occupied by the Applicant. On June 19, 2018, Employment and Social Development Canada/Service Canada sent a letter informing her that she received a positive LMIA.

propositions.text: The LMIA letter stated hiring foreign nationals for the position would likely have a positive or neutral impact on the Canadian labour market.
propositions.quote: The letter states that the “hiring of foreign nationals in the specified occupation and at the specified work location is likely to have a positive or neutral impact on the Canadian labour market.”

paragraphs.summary: The employer applied for and received a positive LMIA stating hiring foreign nationals would likely positively or neutrally impact the Canadian labour market.

propositions.text: The Applicant applied for a temporary work permit on August 3, 2018, including the LMIA number, and indicated no travel in past five years; no financial info was provided.
propositions.quote: On August 3, 2018, the Applicant requested a temporary work permit/visa under the Program so as to begin her employment under the Contract. The LMIA number was included on the visa application form. In her application for temporary residence, the Applicant indicated that she had not travelled to any country or territory in the past five years. The visa application did not contain information pertaining to her assets or available funds.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant applied for a temporary work permit in August 2018, included LMIA number, reported no travel in five years, and provided no financial info.

propositions.text: On November 30, 2018, a visa officer denied the Applicant's temporary work permit application for not meeting IRPA and IRPR requirements.
propositions.quote: In a letter dated November 30, 2018, a visa officer with the Visa Section of the Canadian High Commission in London, United Kingdom, advised the Applicant that her application for a temporary work permit/visa had been denied [the Decision]. The visa officer determined that her application did not meet the requirements of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27, and the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations, SOR/2002-227 [IRPR], for the following reasons:

propositions.text: The visa officer was not satisfied the Applicant would leave Canada after her stay based on travel history, limited employment prospects, and personal assets.
propositions.quote: - I am not satisfied that you will leave Canada at the end of your stay, as stipulated in subsection 216(1) of the IRPR, based on your travel history. - I am not satisfied that you will leave Canada at the end of your stay, as stipulated in subsection 216(1) of the IRPR, based on the limited employment prospects in your country of residence. - I am not satisfied that you will leave Canada at the end of your stay, as stipulated in subsection 216(1) of the IRPR, based on your personal assets and financial status.

paragraphs.summary: The visa officer denied the Applicant's work permit, finding she would not leave Canada based on travel history, employment prospects, and assets.

propositions.text: GCMS notes state Applicant seeks caregiver work, shows no proof of funds/assets or travel history, earns low salary in Nigeria, and is not sufficiently established to motivate return.
propositions.quote: Applicant seeking to work as caregiver, caring for two children under the age of two. Applicant shows no proof of funds/assets, or of previous travel history. Currently working in daycare section of a school, making 20,000 naira (approx. $75 Canadian) per month. Given Applicant’s travel history, funds, and employment opportunities in COR versus in Canada, I am not satisfied that Applicant is sufficiently established to motivate a return to COR at the end of period authorized for stay. For these reasons, application is refused.

paragraphs.summary: GCMS notes show Applicant lacks proof of funds or travel history, earns low salary, and is not sufficiently established to motivate return to home country.

propositions.text: Two issues: (1) Was the visa officer's denial reasonable? (2) Did the visa officer breach procedural fairness by not communicating with the Applicant?
propositions.quote: This application for judicial review raises two issues: (1) Did the visa officer act reasonably in denying the Applicant’s work permit/visa application? (2) Did the visa officer commit a breach of procedural fairness in not communicating with the Applicant to address concerns related to her visa application?

paragraphs.summary: The judicial review raises two issues: reasonableness of denial and procedural fairness regarding communication.

propositions.text: Reasonableness standard requires decision to be within a range of acceptable outcomes defensible on facts and law.
propositions.quote: The first issue engages the reasonableness standard of review, requiring the decision to fall “within a range of possible, acceptable outcomes which are defensible in respect of the facts and law.” In assessing whether it does, this Court must consider whether the decision is justified, transparent, and intelligible (Dunsmuir v New Brunswick, 2008 SCC 9 at para 47 [Dunsmuir]).

paragraphs.summary: Reasonableness review requires the decision to be justified, transparent, and intelligible within acceptable outcomes.

propositions.text: Visa officers' discretionary decisions on temporary work permits get high deference due to factual questions and expertise.
propositions.quote: A visa officer’s assessment for a temporary work permit requires a balancing of many factors. Thus, discretionary decisions of this type are entitled to a high degree of deference since they usually involve questions of fact and relate to a visa officer’s recognized expertise (Singh v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2017 FC 894 at paras 15–16 [Singh]; Portillo v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2014 FC 866 at para 17; Ngalamulume v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2009 FC 1268 at para 16; Talpur v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2012 FC 25 at para 19).

paragraphs.summary: Visa officers' discretionary decisions on work permits deserve high deference due to factual nature and expertise.

propositions.text: Visa officers must provide adequate reasons to justify decisions, allowing courts to understand and assess reasonableness.
propositions.quote: Although a visa officer’s duty to provide reasons when evaluating a temporary resident visa application is minimal, the visa officer must nonetheless provide adequate reasons that justify his or her decision (Singh v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2009 FC 621 at para 9). If the visa officer’s reasons, when read as a whole, “allow the reviewing court to understand why the tribunal made its decision and permit it to determine whether the conclusion is within the range of acceptable outcomes, the Dunsmuir criteria are met” (Newfoundland and Labrador Nurses’ Union v Newfoundland and Labrador (Treasury Board), 2011 SCC 62 at para 16 [NFLD Nurses]; Sibal v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2019 FC 159 at para 22).

paragraphs.summary: Visa officers must provide adequate reasons so courts can understand and assess the decision's reasonableness.

propositions.text: Procedural fairness standard for visa officers' communication is correctness standard.
propositions.quote: Regarding the procedural fairness issue, the standard of review is correctness: Lawal v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2008 FC 861 at paragraph 15; CUPE v Ontario (Minister of Labour), 2003 SCC 29 at paragraph 100; Jin v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2008 FC 1129 at paragraph 13; Bahr v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2012 FC 527 at paragraph 15; Canada (Attorney General) v Sketchley, 2005 FCA 404 at paragraph 53.

paragraphs.summary: The procedural fairness issue is reviewed on a correctness standard.

propositions.text: Visa officers owe a relaxed level of procedural fairness due to the nature of visa application processes.
propositions.quote: However, the level of procedural fairness owed by the visa officer is relaxed, considering the nature of the administrative process for visa applications (Zhang v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2006 FC 1381 at para 37 [Zhang]; Zhou v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2013 FC 465 at para 21 [Zhou]).

paragraphs.summary: Visa officers owe a relaxed procedural fairness level given the administrative nature of visa applications.

propositions.text: The Applicant argues the visa officer failed to consider her employment history and letter of recommendation, misconstrued her application, and erred in negative inference from lack of travel history.
propositions.quote: The Applicant submits that the visa officer’s decision and reasoning is problematic. She argues that the visa officer failed to give weight to her previous employment history in Nigeria and her letter of recommendation, misconstrued the nature of the Applicant’s work permit application, and erred in drawing a negative inference from the Applicant’s lack of travel history. In essence, the Applicant argues that the visa officer was not alive to what was before him and failed to provide sufficient reasons to justify his decision to reject the Applicant’s visa application.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant argues the visa officer failed to consider key evidence and erred in reasoning, providing insufficient reasons.

propositions.text: The Respondent argues the visa officer considered relevant factors and reasonably refused the application, noting officers need not provide detailed reasons.
propositions.quote: The Respondent argues that the visa officer considered all of the relevant factors and rendered a reasonable decision. The Respondent argues that the visa officer was reasonable when he considered the Applicant’s low salary in Nigeria, her status as a single woman, and the economic conditions in Nigeria when deciding to refuse the Applicant’s work permit application. The Respondent further states that visa officers are not required to provide detailed reasons in support of their decisions.

paragraphs.summary: The Respondent argues the visa officer reasonably considered relevant factors and need not provide detailed reasons.

propositions.text: Deficiencies in reasons are closely linked to reasonableness review as clarified by the Supreme Court in NFLD Nurses.
propositions.quote: The first issue relates to the sufficiency of the reasons. As the Supreme Court clarified in NFLD Nurses at paragraph 21, issues related to “alleged deficiencies or flaws in the reasons” given by an administrative decision-maker are intimately associated with reasonableness review.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes that alleged deficiencies in reasons relate closely to reasonableness review per Supreme Court guidance.

propositions.text: Applicants bear burden to rebut presumption they are immigrants and to convince visa officers they will leave Canada after stay.
propositions.quote: In addition, the burden is upon visa applicants to rebut the presumption that they are immigrants seeking to remain in Canada, and to convince a visa officer that they will leave Canada at the end of their stay (Danioko v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2006 FC 479 at para 15; Li v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2001 FCT 791, [2001] FCJ No 1144 (QL) at para 35 [Li]; Fakhri Adhari v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2017 FC 854 at para 29).

paragraphs.summary: Applicants must rebut the presumption of immigrant intent and convince visa officers they will leave Canada after their stay.

propositions.text: Several guideposts for analysis: presumption of immigrant intent, no re-weighing evidence, officer presumed to review all evidence, no need to reference every document, reasons include form, letter, and GCMS notes.
propositions.quote: As set out in Mohammed v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2017 FC 992 at para 13: There are several guideposts for this analysis which are clearly established: (1) there is a legal presumption according to which any person seeking to enter Canada is presumed to be an immigrant; it is up to the applicant to rebut this presumption: Danioko v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2006 FC 479 at para 15; (2) it is not for the Court to re-weigh the evidence; (3) the Officer is presumed to have reviewed all of the evidence unless the contrary is shown (Florea v Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration), [1993] FCJ No 598 (QL) (FCA)) and is not required to make reference to every document submitted (Hassan v Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration) (1992), 147 NR 317, [1992] FCJ No 946 (QL) (FCA); Zhou v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2013 FC 465 at para 20; (4) the Officer’s reasons for decision include the form and the letter, as well as the GCMS notes prepared for the case.

paragraphs.summary: The court outlines guideposts: presumption of immigrant intent, no re-weighing, officer presumed to review all evidence, and reasons include form, letter, and GCMS notes.

propositions.text: Visa officer found Applicant did not meet burden to show she would leave Canada after work contract.
propositions.quote: the visa officer found that the Applicant did not meet her burden to show that she would leave Canada at the end of her work contract.

propositions.text: Decision based on Applicant's lack of funds, absence of travel history, and poor employment prospects in Nigeria.
propositions.quote: This determination was made on the basis of the Applicant’s lack of evidence of funds, absence of travel history, and poor employment prospects in Nigeria.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker found the Applicant failed to prove she would leave Canada, citing lack of funds, travel history, and poor employment prospects.

propositions.text: Visa officers commonly use templates and have wide discretion, including considering objective criteria.
propositions.quote: I accept that it has become commonplace for visa officers to use templates in rendering their decisions... visa officers enjoy a wide berth of discretion in making their decisions and may take into account objective criteria

paragraphs.summary: The court accepts visa officers use templates and have broad discretion including objective criteria.

propositions.text: Visa officers using templates must modify reasons to show intelligible thought process and address contradictory evidence.
propositions.quote: when using templates, visa officers should bring the necessary modifications or render reasons that would indicate their thought process in an intelligible manner, and address evidence that may contradict important findings of fact.

propositions.text: Visa officer did not explain how evidence was interpreted to reach decision.
propositions.quote: the visa officer did not establish the basis for understanding how he interpreted the evidence to arrive at his decision.

paragraphs.summary: The court rules visa officers must explain reasoning intelligibly; here, the visa officer failed to do so.

propositions.text: Visa officer's reasons are hurried and do not explain decision process.
propositions.quote: The visa officer’s reasons are rather hurried, and do not explain the thought process that underlies his decision to refuse the work visa.

propositions.text: Decision incorrectly references subsection 216(1) IRPR (study permits) instead of section 200 (work permits).
propositions.quote: the Decision makes reference to subsection 216(1) of the IRPR, which relates to study permits, rather than to section 200 of the IRPR, which relates to work permits.

propositions.text: This error suggests inattention but is not fatal as GCMS Notes align with work permit criteria.
propositions.quote: Although this may suggest inattention and a hurried approach, in and of itself it is not fatal in this case as the remarks in the GCMS Notes seem to be in line with work permit application criteria.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the visa officer's reasons hurried and notes a legislative reference error, but this is not fatal here.

propositions.text: The Decision suffers from a series of shortcomings.
propositions.quote: That said, the Decision does suffer from a series of shortcomings.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Decision has several shortcomings.

propositions.text: Visa officer failed to give sufficient weight to Applicant's reasonable employment history in Nigeria.
propositions.quote: the visa officer failed to give sufficient weight to evidence showing that the Applicant had a reasonable employment history in Nigeria.

propositions.text: GCMS Notes mention Applicant's employment and positive letter of recommendation, training certificates, and over three years employment.
propositions.quote: In the GCMS Notes, there is a brief mention of the Applicant’s employment in Nigeria... positive letter of recommendation... training certificates and over three years of employment in Nigeria.

propositions.text: These factors could displace finding of poor employment prospects but visa officer did not address them.
propositions.quote: These are all relevant factors which may well go to displacing a finding that the Applicant had poor employment prospects in Nigeria.

propositions.text: Visa officer should have specifically addressed Applicant's employment history given its significance.
propositions.quote: it seems to me that the visa officer in this case should have specifically addressed the Applicant’s current employment history.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the visa officer ignored relevant employment evidence that could counter poor prospects finding.

propositions.text: Visa officer drew negative inference from Applicant's salary without contextualizing its sufficiency for living standards in Nigeria.
propositions.quote: visa officer states that the Applicant makes “20,000 naira... without any further explanation as to whether this salary is sufficient to maintain a reasonable standard of living

propositions.text: Visa officers may use general knowledge but must contextualize salary against local living standards.
propositions.quote: While visa officers may use their general knowledge and expertise... there is nothing in the GCMS Notes that contextualizes the Applicant’s salary in Nigeria against living standards in that country.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the visa officer negatively inferred from salary without proper context of local living standards.

propositions.text: Better job opportunities in Canada are common for applicants from lower standard of living countries.
propositions.quote: such is the case for most applicants in similar circumstances coming from countries with a significantly lower standard of living than Canada.

propositions.text: Visa officer's failure to address stable employment history and salary comments makes conclusion unjustified and unintelligible.
propositions.quote: By simply stating the Applicant’s salary without any comment... makes it very difficult to say that the conclusion of the visa officer is justified, transparent and intelligible

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the visa officer's conclusion unjustified due to failure to address employment history and salary context.

propositions.text: Visa officer cited Applicant's limited funds but did not consider job offer in Canada with salary and benefits.
propositions.quote: visa officer also cites the Applicant’s limited funds... but without any mention of the fact that the Applicant is coming to Canada with a job in hand

propositions.text: Court cannot assess visa officer's reasoning without comment on how job offer affects sufficiency of funds criterion.
propositions.quote: I cannot assess the visa officer’s reasoning without further comment on his part on how the job in hand in Canada would not otherwise render the criterion of the sufficiency of funds as having been met.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the visa officer failed to consider the job offer's impact on funds sufficiency and did not explain reasoning.

propositions.text: Further comment on funds sufficiency may not be needed for study permits but is needed here for work permit.
propositions.quote: I accept that further comment would not be necessary in the case of a study permit under subsection 216(1) of the IRPR, but I would think it would be in a case such as this one.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds further comment on funds sufficiency necessary for work permit cases like this one.

propositions.text: Lack of travel history should be treated as neutral factor in likelihood of returning to country.
propositions.quote: The Federal Court has consistently held that a work permit applicant’s lack of travel history should be treated as a neutral factor

propositions.text: Cases Ogunfowora, Huang, Adom hold lack of travel history is neutral in return likelihood.
propositions.quote: see Ogunfowora v Canada... Huang v Canada... Adom v Canada...

paragraphs.summary: The court states prior cases hold lack of travel history is a neutral factor in return likelihood.

propositions.text: It is an error to use lack of travel history as negative factor in determining likelihood of leaving Canada.
propositions.quote: It is thus an error for a visa officer to use the Applicant’s lack of previous travel history as a negative factor

paragraphs.summary: The court finds it erroneous to use lack of travel history as a negative factor for leaving Canada.

propositions.text: Visa officer has discretion to assign weight to evidence.
propositions.quote: I agree with the Respondent that it is within the visa officer’s discretion to assign degree of weight to the evidence

propositions.text: Visa officer should articulate reasons to allow court to assess justification, transparency, intelligibility.
propositions.quote: the visa officer should have in this case articulated even short reasons so as to allow this Court to assess whether the overall outcome fits “comfortably within the principles of justification, transparency and intelligibility”

paragraphs.summary: The respondent argues visa officer has discretion; the court says reasons must be articulated for assessment.

propositions.text: Visa officer was not attuned to nature and content of Applicant’s work permit application.
propositions.quote: I find that the visa officer was not attuned to the nature and content of the Applicant’s work permit application.

propositions.text: Court understands what visa officer says but not why; understanding why is important.
propositions.quote: Although I understand what the visa officer is saying, I do not understand why he is saying it; it is important that I do.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the visa officer misunderstood the application and failed to explain reasoning adequately.

propositions.text: Visa officer should have called Applicant to respond to concerns before rejecting application.
propositions.quote: the Applicant argues that the visa officer should have at least made a telephone call to the Applicant so as to allow her to respond to his concerns

propositions.text: Applicant cites Wang case supporting duty to communicate concerns before refusal.
propositions.quote: Citing Wang v Canada... the Applicant argues...

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant argues, citing Wang, that the visa officer should have contacted her to address concerns before refusal.

propositions.text: Visa application process has relaxed duty of fairness due to absence of legal right and burden on applicant.
propositions.quote: the duty of fairness regarding the visa application process is relaxed... absence of a legal right to a visa; the imposition on the Applicant of the burden of establishing eligibility

propositions.text: FCA in Khan explained factors limiting duty of fairness and cautioned against procedural formality that impedes efficiency.
propositions.quote: The FCA explained... several factors account for this limited duty of fairness... cautioned against imposing a level of procedural formality that... would unduly encumber efficient administration

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the visa process has a relaxed fairness duty, per FCA in Khan, to preserve efficiency.

propositions.text: Additional communication may be appropriate if doubts about credibility, extrinsic evidence, or stereotypes arise.
propositions.quote: Additional communication with a visa applicant may be appropriate... where the visa officer harbours doubts as to the credibility... or relies on extrinsic evidence... or relies on overly broad generalizations or stereotypes

propositions.text: Cases Salman and Hassani support communication when credibility or extrinsic evidence concerns exist.
propositions.quote: see Salman v Canada... Hassani v Canada...

paragraphs.summary: The court states communication may be needed if credibility or extrinsic evidence concerns arise, citing Salman and Hassani.

propositions.text: Wang case found telephone call appropriate to allow response to concerns about sincerity and bona fides.
propositions.quote: In that case, this Court found that the visa officer should have provided the Applicant with an opportunity to respond to concerns about the “sincerity of [the Applicant’s] cousin’s offer of support, and [the Applicant’s] bona fides as a temporary visitor to Canada”

paragraphs.summary: The Wang case held a telephone call was appropriate to allow response to sincerity and bona fides concerns.

propositions.text: Visa officer must inform Applicant when extrinsic evidence is used to support decision.
propositions.quote: A visa officer should also inform the Applicant of his or her concerns when he or she obtains extrinsic evidence that may be used to support the final decision

paragraphs.summary: Visa officers must inform applicants when extrinsic evidence supports the decision, per Ali case.

propositions.text: Visa officers may not rely on cultural or regional generalizations without allowing applicant to respond.
propositions.quote: visa officers may not justify their decisions on cultural or regional generalizations without allowing the applicant to respond

propositions.text: Cases Yuan and Hernandez Bonilla hold applicants must be allowed to respond to generalizations.
propositions.quote: Yuan v Canada... Hernandez Bonilla v Canada...

paragraphs.summary: Visa officers cannot rely on cultural generalizations without allowing response, per Yuan and Hernandez Bonilla.

propositions.text: This Court has consistently rejected the argument that an applicant has the right to clarify or respond to the visa officer's decision, except in certain exceptions.
propositions.quote: this Court has consistently rejected the argument that an applicant has the right to clarify his or her application or respond to the merits of the visa officer’s decision

paragraphs.summary: The court states it has consistently rejected the argument that an applicant can clarify or respond to the visa officer's decision except in certain exceptions.

propositions.text: The present case does not fall within exceptions requiring heightened duty of fairness.
propositions.quote: The factual circumstances of the present case do not fall within one of the exceptions that give rise to a heightened duty of fairness

propositions.text: No evidence suggests the visa officer doubted the applicant's credibility or relied on broad generalizations.
propositions.quote: There is no evidence to suggest that the visa officer had doubts as to the credibility, veracity, or sincerity of the Applicant’s evidence or that he relied upon broad generalizations about the Applicant’s personal characteristics or country of origin

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no exceptions apply and no evidence of visa officer doubting applicant's credibility or relying on generalizations.

propositions.text: The visa officer did not err in not providing the applicant an opportunity to further justify her visa application.
propositions.quote: I find that the visa officer did not err in not providing the Applicant with an opportunity to further justify her visa application

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes the visa officer did not err by not giving the applicant a chance to further justify her application.

propositions.text: The visa officer did not provide a sufficiently clear indication of the basis for his decision.
propositions.quote: the visa officer did not provide a sufficiently clear indication of the basis for his decision

propositions.text: The reasons given fail to allow determination if the conclusion is within acceptable outcomes.
propositions.quote: the reasons given fail to allow me to determine whether the conclusion reached is within the range of acceptable outcomes

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the visa officer's reasons unclear and insufficient to determine if the decision was acceptable.

propositions.text: The application for judicial review is allowed, the visa officer's decision is set aside, and the matter is remitted to a different officer.
propositions.quote: The application for judicial review is allowed, the decision of the visa officer is set aside and the matter is remitted to a different officer for redetermination

propositions.text: No certified question was submitted or arose.
propositions.quote: The parties did not submit a certified question and none arose

propositions.text: The judgment and reasons are dated September 30, 2019, heard in Montréal, Quebec, with appearances for applicant and respondent noted.
propositions.quote: JUDGMENT AND reasons: PAMEL J. DATED: september 30, 2019 APPEARANCES: Me Marie-Maude R. Beauvais Me Idorenyin E. Amana For The Applicant Me Lynne Lazaroff For The Respondent

propositions.text: Solicitors of record are Amana Law Office for the applicant and Attorney General of Canada for the respondent.
propositions.quote: SOLICITORS OF RECORD: Amana Law Office Cornwall, Ontario For The Applicant Attorney General of Canada Montréal, Quebec For The Respondent

paragraphs.summary: The court allows judicial review, sets aside the visa officer's decision, remits the matter, notes no certified question, and records hearing details and counsel.
